teaser.text: Prologis is a landlord for the physical systems that move goods from producers to customers. Its dollar begins as rent and related payments, then passes through property costs, financing, investment and shareholder distributions.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for Prologis?

paragraphs.text: The bear case gives $4,650 million in both October 2027 and October 2028, then $4,700 million in October 2029. Weaker leasing, concessions, financing costs and transaction dilution absorb operating improvement. The bull case gives $5,100 million, then $5,550 million, and finally $6,050 million. It requires faster rent capture, improving occupancy, successful development and contracted data-center projects.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Prologis really make?

paragraphs.text: The annual table’s row labelled AFFO presents Prologis’s Core FFO measure. Prologis reports AFFO separately: it removes noncash rent and deducts property improvements and turnover costs, while making other specified adjustments. In 2025, Core FFO was $5.81 per share against a dividend of $4.04. The displayed payout was 69.5%, but that does not mean the remaining 30.5% was free cash after every building obligation.

Consolidated operating cash flow was approximately $5,008 million in 2025. The AFFO reconciliation deducted $327.355 million of property improvements and $562.197 million of turnover costs. These costs prepare buildings for tenants and preserve their earning capacity. Development spending is different from maintenance, so deducting every capital dollar would also understate expansion.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for Prologis today?

paragraphs.text: Today’s price assumes Prologis can turn a large property base into growing cash flow per share. The current AFFO multiple implies about $6.16 of AFFO per share, while the implied earnings yield is about 4.9%. A ten-year US government bond yielded 5.090%, which helps explain why investors care about both income and growth.

blocks.heading: How much does Prologis pay per share?

paragraphs.text: The annual table’s row labelled AFFO presents Prologis’s Core FFO measure. Prologis reports AFFO separately: it removes noncash rent and deducts property improvements and turnover costs, while making other specified adjustments. In 2025, Core FFO was $5.81 per share against a dividend of $4.04. The displayed payout was 69.5%, but that does not mean the remaining 30.5% was free cash after every building obligation.

The current annualized dividend is $4.28 after the latest increase. The base case pays $4.41, $4.67 and $4.95, reflecting a roughly 5% initial increase followed by 6% annual increases. Coverage supports moderation: 2025 AFFO per share was $5.81 against a $4.04 dividend. The bear case holds each period at $4.28 because leverage and weaker leasing could pause increases. The bull case pays $4.45, $4.76 and $5.09, requiring 7% annual increases.

blocks.heading: Is Prologis’s dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: Development and capital spending, together with acquisitions, required more than the cash left after dividends. Prologis filled that gap by selling properties and issuing debt. This is like a household whose wages cover groceries but not a house extension: it must save, sell an asset or borrow. The dividend was supportable, but expansion depended on recycling capital and using financing.

blocks.heading: What has Prologis guided for the year?

paragraphs.text: Management’s October 15 guidance puts full-year net earnings at $4.05–$4.15 per diluted share. It puts Core FFO at $6.25–$6.29 per share. Core FFO adjusts accounting earnings for building depreciation, property-sale gains and other specified items, so it better reflects recurring property performance.

The operating promise has improved. Prologis now expects cash same-store NOI growth of 7.0%–7.5%. NOI means net operating income: property revenue less property expenses, before corporate overhead and financing. “Same-store” means the comparison follows a consistent group of properties rather than growth from buying more buildings.

blocks.heading: Has Prologis kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Management also met its operating forecast. Core FFO, an adjusted property-company earnings measure that removes depreciation and certain property-sale gains, reached US$5.81 per share in 2025, the top of the forecast range. That supports execution credibility, but Core FFO is not cash in the bank and does not prove every investment earned an adequate return.

blocks.heading: What do Prologis’s last eight quarters show?

paragraphs.text: Revenue and NOI grew at nearly the same rate year over year, suggesting that property operations supplied most of the quarter’s improvement. Revenue nevertheless fell from the second quarter, when promote revenue had been stronger. The sequential decline therefore says little by itself about rents.

blocks.heading: What should Prologis watchers look for next?

paragraphs.text: December 31, 2026 results should show whether Prologis delivered its stronger property-income forecast and increased construction program. Investors should compare starts with leasing commitments, cash spent with progress, and asset-sale proceeds with the capital-recycling plan.
